'''Nicholas B. Lydon''' [[Royal Society|FRS]] (born 27 February 1957) is a British scientist and entrepreneur.<ref name="heroes">{{cite web |url=http://www.scienceheroes.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=379&Itemid=312 |title=Nicholas Lydon |website=www.scienceheroes.com |year=2010 |access-date=13 February 2013}}</ref> In 2009, he was awarded the [[Lasker Award|Lasker Clinical Award]] and in 2012 the [[Japan Prize]] for the development of [[Imatinib|Gleevec]], also known as Imatinib, a selective BCR-ABL inhibitor for the treatment of [[chronic myeloid leukaemia]] (CML), which converted a fatal cancer into a manageable chronic condition.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.laskerfoundation.org/awards/2009_c_description.htm|title=Lasker – DeBakey Clinical Medical Research Award: Award Description|publisher=[[Albert Lasker|Lasker Foundation]]|access-date=16 August 2010}}</ref><ref name="japan">{{cite web |url=http://www.japanprize.jp/en/prize_prof_2012_b_lydon.html |title=Laureates of the Japan Prize |publisher=[[Japan Prize|The Japan Prize Foundation]] |year=2012 |access-date=13 February 2013}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Druker | first1 = B. ==Education==
Lydon was educated at [[Strathallan School]] near [[Perth (Scotland)|Perth]], [[Scotland]].<ref name="dundee">{{cite web |url=http://www.ppu.mrc.ac.uk/resources/Nick_Lydon_Laureation.doc |title=Dr Nicholas Lydon |publisher=University of Dundee |year=2011 |access-date=13 February 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130517065457/http://www.ppu.mrc.ac.uk/resources/Nick_Lydon_Laureation.doc |archive-date=17 May 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He earned a Bachelor of Science degree in [[biochemistry]] from the [[University of Leeds]], [[England]] in 1978 and received his PhD in biochemistry from the [[University of Dundee]], Scotland in 1982.<ref name="dundee" /><ref name="lydonphd">{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=Nicholas B.|last=Lydon |title=Studies on the hormone-sensitive adenylate cyclase from bovine corpus luteum |publisher=[[University of Dundee]] |date=1982 |url=http://www.theses.com|author-link=Nicholas Lydon}}{{subscription required}}</ref>

==Career==
In 1982, Lydon accepted a position with [[Schering-Plough]] based in [[France]] as Chargé de Récherche.<ref name="japan" /> Three years later, he moved to Switzerland to work with [[Novartis|Ciba-Geigy Pharmaceuticals]], with whom he developed Gleevec.<ref name="dundee" /> In 1997, he established Kinetex Pharmaceuticals in Boston which was acquired by [[Amgen]] in 2000, with whom he worked until 2002.<ref name="dundee" /> Thereafter, he established several companies that continue to develop drugs to treat various conditions.<ref name="dundee" />

==Honours and awards==

*  [[Warren Alpert Foundation Prize]], 2000.<ref name="japan" />
*  Twenty First Annual [[AACR Awards|AACR-Bruce F. Cain Memorial Award]], 2002.<ref name="japan" />
*  Charles F. [[Kettering Prize]], General Motors Cancer Research Foundation, 2002.<ref name="japan" />
*  The [[Lasker-DeBakey Clinical Medical Research Award]], with [[Brian Druker]] and [[Charles Sawyers]], 2009.<ref name="japan" />
*  The [[Japan Prize]], with Brian Druker and [[Janet Rowley]], 2012.<ref name="japan" />
*  [[Fellow of the Royal Society]], 2013.<ref name="royal">{{cite web |url=http://royalsociety.org/people/nicholas-lydon/ |title=Dr Nicholas Lydon |publisher=[[Royal Society]] |date=2013 |access-date=29 May 2013}}</ref>
*  [[GlaxoSmithKline Prize|Royal Society GlaxoSmithKline Prize and Lecture]], 2014<ref>{{cite web| url = http://royalsociety.org/awards/glaxosmithkline-prize-lecture/|title= GlaxoSmithKline prize|publisher=Royal Society|access-date = 12 September 2013}}</ref>

Lydon's nomination for the [[Royal Society]] reads: {{centred pull quote|Nick Lydon played a decisive role in the development of [[Imatinib|Gleevec (Imatinib)]], a drug that has saved the lives of thousands of patients with [[Chronic myelogenous leukemia|chronic myelogenous leukaemia (CML)]] and [[Gastrointestinal stromal tumor|gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GIST)]]. Gleevec revolutionised the field of cancer [[drug discovery]] by changing rapidly fatal diseases into easily treatable conditions, and showed that, by targeting an [[oncogene]] that is the molecular cause of a specific cancer, the defective cancer cells can be killed without any major side effects on normal cells. The remarkable efficacy of Gleevec profoundly changed the perception of [[protein kinase]]s as therapeutic targets. From being considered to be virtually "[[Druggability|undruggable]]" in 1994, they have become the pharmaceutical industry's most popular class of drug target today, accounting for over 50% of cancer drug discovery [[Research and development|R&D]]. The international prizes that Nick Lydon has received include, most recently, the Lasker-DeBakey Clinical Medical Research Award from The Lasker Foundation.<ref name="royal"/>}}
